prompt.context: Marie's Café is a small local coffee shop that serves coffee. Marie's has been around for decades and is known for its high quality drinks and cozy atmosphere. The café has seen declining profits over the last few quarters, and the owner has hired you to increase its profits. There are two other coffee shops nearby that sell coffees and pastries — no further information is available on them. Marie's currently serves two items (coffee and latte) in three different sizes.
prompt.question: What are the reasons for Marie's Café's declining profits, and how would you increase its profits?

clarifying_info.q: What products does Marie's sell and at what prices?
clarifying_info.a: Marie's sells coffee and lattes in 8 oz, 12 oz, and 16 oz sizes. See Exhibit 1 for prices, costs, and customer purchase mix.

clarifying_info.q: What are the café's operating hours?
clarifying_info.a: 7am to 10pm, Monday through Friday. Closed on weekends.

clarifying_info.q: How many baristas work at any given time?
clarifying_info.a: Two baristas are working at any given time, each paid $15/hr.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to serve one customer?
clarifying_info.a: On average, it takes 2 minutes for a barista to complete an order.

clarifying_info.q: What happens if customers can't be served quickly?
clarifying_info.a: Customers leave if they cannot be served quickly.

exhibits.title: Products, Costs, and Customer Splits
exhibits.shows: A table listing all six products (Coffee 8 oz, 12 oz, 16 oz; Latte 8 oz, 12 oz, 16 oz) with their price, cost breakdown (cups and ingredients sold separately), and percentage of customer purchases. Note: food and packaging costs are separate.

exhibits.title: Demand of Coffee per Hour
exhibits.shows: A table showing average customer demand per hour across five time blocks during the operating day.

framework: Market: Assess market growth trends and changing consumer preferences (product mix, atmosphere)
Competition: Identify new low-cost competitors or substitutes (restaurants, fast food chains) nearby
Company – Customers: Evaluate foot traffic and number of customers served
Company – Operations: Analyze process efficiency (avg. time per customer) and total café capacity
Product: Review product diversification, pricing sensitivity, complementary services (e.g. Wi-Fi), and brand/quality image

questions.prompt: Question 1: How much profit does Marie's Café currently make per customer? (Assume each customer purchases only one drink per visit.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate unit profit for each product (price minus cup cost minus ingredient cost), then weight by customer purchase percentages. Strong candidates will note that larger sizes yield higher gross profit per transaction and suggest strategies such as promoting larger sizes, introducing a 20 oz option, or eliminating the 8 oz size.

math.setup: Unit Profit = Price - Cup Cost - Ingredient Cost; Avg Profit per Customer = sum of (Unit Profit × % of Customer Purchases)
steps: Coffee 8 oz: $1.00 - $0.30 - $0.10 = $0.60 unit profit × 15% = $0.08 (rounded) → actually $1.00-$0.50=$0.50 per casebook; see note
Coffee 8 oz (per casebook cost $0.50): $1.00 - $0.50 = $0.50 unit profit × 15% = $0.075 ≈ $0.08
math.answer: Average profit ≈ $1.50 per customer. Casebook product costs (combining cup + ingredient): Coffee 8 oz = $0.50, Coffee 12 oz = $0.70, Coffee 16 oz = $0.90; Latte 8 oz = $1.30, Latte 12 oz = $1.90, Latte 16 oz = $2.50.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What is the average profit that Marie's Café earns per day? (Two baristas at any time, paid $15/hr; hours 7am–10pm Mon–Fri; 2 min per order; customers leave if not served quickly.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must determine how many customers each set of baristas can serve per hour (each barista handles 30 customers/hr at 2 min/order, so 2 baristas = 60/hr), cap served customers at demand, compute revenue profit using $1.50/customer, then subtract barista cost ($15/hr × 2 = $30/hr). Candidate should notice that evening hours are unprofitable with 2 baristas (15 customers × $1.50 = $22.50 revenue vs $30 cost) and recommend adjusting staffing. With 2 baristas throughout, daily profit = $607.50. Optimizing barista count by time block yields $787.50.

math.setup: Capacity per barista = 60 min/hr ÷ 2 min/order = 30 customers/hr. With N baristas: capacity = 30N. Served = min(demand, capacity). Profit per block = (hours in block) × (served × $1.50 - baristas × $15).
steps: Barista capacity: 30 customers/hr each; 2 baristas = 60/hr capacity
Optimal staffing — 7AM–10AM 3 baristas (capacity 90): served 90, profit/hr = 90×$1.50 - 3×$15 = $135 - $45 = $90; block = $270
4PM–7PM 1 barista (capacity 30): served 30 or 40 (casebook shows 1 or 2 baristas); with 1 barista served=30, profit/hr=30×$1.50-1×$15=$30; block=$90
math.answer: With 2 baristas throughout: $607.50/day. With optimal barista scheduling: $787.50/day.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Brainstorm): One of Marie's competitors sells pastries. What factors should Marie's Café consider before purchasing an oven to sell pastries?
questions.guidance: Candidate should organize considerations across revenue, costs, capacity, brand, and competitive dimensions. Strong candidates weigh both pros and cons of each factor.

questions.prompt: Question 4: A new espresso machine priced at $2,000 can decrease order time from 2 minutes to 90 seconds. How long would it take to pay back the machine?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate daily profit with the new 90-second order time (each barista now handles 40 customers/hr), determine the incremental daily profit vs. the optimized baseline from Question 2 ($787.50), and divide machine cost by incremental daily profit. Machine payback = $2,000 ÷ ($922.50 - $787.50) = $2,000 ÷ $135 ≈ 14.8 days. Candidate should also note that peak-hour baristas yield similar profits and fewer turned-away customers.

math.setup: New capacity per barista = 60 min ÷ 1.5 min/order = 40 customers/hr. Recalculate served and profit per block with optimal baristas. Payback = machine cost ÷ (new optimal daily profit - old optimal daily profit).
steps: 7AM–10AM 3 baristas: capacity 120 ≥ demand 100; served 100, profit/hr=100×$1.50-3×$15=$150-$45=$105; block=$315
10AM–1PM 2 baristas: capacity 80 = demand 80; served 80, profit/hr=80×$1.50-2×$15=$120-$30=$90; block=$270
1PM–4PM 2 baristas: capacity 80 ≥ demand 60; served 60, profit/hr=$60; block=$180
4PM–7PM 1 barista: capacity 40 = demand 40; served 40, profit/hr=40×$1.50-1×$15=$60-$15=$45; block=$135
7PM–10PM 1 barista: capacity 40 ≥ demand 15; served 15, profit/hr=15×$1.50-$15=$7.50; block=$22.50
math.answer: Approximately 14.8 days to pay back the $2,000 machine.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should Marie's Café consider before purchasing an oven to sell pastries?

categories.name: Revenue
ideas: Incremental doughnut/pastry sales
Increased synergies — higher ticket per customer pairing coffee with pastry
Higher foot traffic if pastry offering draws new customers

categories.name: Fixed Costs
ideas: Purchase price of oven
Installation and setup
Display case purchase/setup
Storage space build-out
Advertising and menu changes

categories.name: Variable Costs
ideas: Ingredients for pastries
Hiring and training additional staff to bake
Packaging for pastries

categories.name: Capacity
ideas: Physical space in café for oven and ingredient storage
Barista bandwidth to handle increased demand
Kitchen workflow impact on coffee service speed

categories.name: Brand & Quality
ideas: Marie's is known for coffee quality and cozy atmosphere — pastries could enhance or dilute brand
Low-quality pastries could alienate loyal customers
Premium pastries could reinforce premium positioning

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Competitor already sells pastries — pricing and quality benchmark
Risk of being seen as copycat vs. differentiated offering

categories.name: Alternative Options
ideas: Purchase ready-made pastries from a wholesaler or bakery instead of baking in-house (lower fixed cost, faster launch)
Partner with a local bakery

recommendation: Focus on driving profits through larger drink sizes (16 oz) which yield higher gross profit per transaction — promote upsizing and consider eliminating 8 oz sizes
Optimize barista scheduling: add a third barista during peak morning hours (7–10AM) and reduce to one barista during slow evening hours (7–10PM) to increase daily profit from $607.50 to $787.50
Invest in the new espresso machine ($2,000) — it pays back in ~14.8 days and increases optimal daily profit to $922.50
Diversify product range by adding food/pastries — consider sourcing from a wholesaler first to minimize fixed costs while testing demand
Explore complementary services such as Wi-Fi to increase customer dwell time and revenue per visit
risks: Adding Wi-Fi may increase dwell time and reduce table turnover, straining already limited café capacity
Hiring additional baristas may be difficult; staffing flexibility during peak vs. off-peak times must be managed carefully
Introducing in-house baked pastries risks brand dilution if quality is inconsistent — wholesaler option mitigates this
next_steps: Model full P&L impact of eliminating 8 oz sizes and promoting 16 oz across both product lines
Pilot the espresso machine purchase given ~15-day payback and measure actual throughput improvement
Get quotes from local wholesalers for pastry supply and run a 30-day trial before committing to oven purchase
Evaluate Wi-Fi feasibility given current café layout and seating capacity
